questions.question: What is Dependency Injection (DI) and why do we need it?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Dependency Injection is a design pattern where a class receives its dependencies from an external source — the IoC (Inversion of Control) container — rather than creating them itself with new. The class declares what it needs (usually via its constructor) and the container supplies a ready-made instance at resolution time.

✅ Advantages

  • Loose coupling — a class depends on an interface, not a concrete implementation, so implementations can be swapped without touching consumers
  • Testability — real services can be replaced with mocks/fakes in unit tests without changing production code
  • Lifetime management — the container decides when objects are created, shared, and disposed
  • Single Responsibility — classes focus on their own logic instead of on constructing their collaborators

💻 Examples

ASP.NET Core ships a built-in DI container configured in Program.cs:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IAuthService, AuthService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<DashboardService>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<FundHoldingsService>();

// Constructor injection — DI resolves automatically
public DashboardController(DashboardService dashboardService)
{
    _dashboardService = dashboardService;
}

🎯 Uses

  • Wiring up services, repositories, and infrastructure in every ASP.NET Core app via Program.cs
  • Swapping a real implementation for a mock/stub in unit tests
  • Swapping environment-specific implementations (e.g. a fake email sender in Development vs SMTP in Production)
  • Decoupling business logic from framework/infrastructure concerns (databases, HTTP clients, caches)

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Dependency Injection is a pattern where an object's dependencies are supplied by an external container instead of being created internally with new. It's the concrete implementation of the Inversion of Control principle. The main benefits are loose coupling — my classes depend on interfaces, not concrete types — and testability, since I can inject mocks in unit tests. In .NET, IServiceCollection is the container: I register a service once in Program.cs and every class that needs it just declares it as a constructor parameter; the framework resolves and injects it automatically. One real gap I've seen in production code is injecting concrete classes instead of interfaces (e.g. AuthService instead of IAuthService) — that defeats the purpose of DI because you can no longer swap the implementation for testing.

projectExample.explanation: In FolioTrack, every service is registered in Program.cs. DashboardController never calls 'new DashboardService()'. The DI container resolves and injects it automatically. One gap we identified: most services are injected as concrete classes, not interfaces — ideally should be IAuthService, not AuthService, for proper mocking.

followUps.question: What is the difference between DI (pattern) and IoC (principle)?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Inversion of Control (IoC) is a broad design principle: instead of your code controlling the creation of its dependencies, control is handed to an external authority — "don't call us, we'll call you" (the Hollywood Principle). Dependency Injection is one specific technique that implements IoC by pushing dependencies into a class from outside (constructor, property, or method) rather than the class pulling them via new.

✅ Advantages

  • Separates what a class needs from how that dependency is created and wired up
  • Makes the codebase easier to reason about — construction logic lives in one place (the container), not scattered across classes
  • Enables other IoC techniques (Service Locator, Template Method, events) to be compared and understood on the same footing
  • Constructor-injection DI is the cleanest, most testable form of IoC compared to alternatives like Service Locator

💻 Examples

// IoC principle in action: PaymentService does NOT create its dependency
public class PaymentService(IPaymentGateway gateway) // DI is the mechanism
{
    public Task ChargeAsync(decimal amount) => gateway.ChargeAsync(amount);
}

// The container (IoC) decides which gateway to hand over
builder.Services.AddScoped<IPaymentGateway, RazorpayGateway>();

🎯 Uses

  • Explaining architecture decisions in design reviews — DI is the tool, IoC is the reasoning behind it
  • Comparing DI against alternative IoC mechanisms like Service Locator or event-driven callbacks
  • Justifying why constructor injection is preferred in .NET over manual object graphs

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

IoC is the principle, DI is one implementation of it. IoC says a class shouldn't control the creation of its own dependencies — control is inverted to an external party. DI is the specific mechanism .NET uses: the container calls my constructor and passes in what it needs. Other IoC implementations exist, like Service Locator or the Template Method pattern, but constructor-injection DI is the cleanest because dependencies stay explicit and testable. In .NET, IServiceCollection is the IoC container and constructor injection is the DI mechanism it uses.

questions.tip: Always inject the interface, not the concrete class (e.g., IAuthService, not AuthService). This enables mocking in unit tests. Mention the captive dependency anti-pattern — it shows you've faced real-world DI issues.

questions.question: Explain the three service lifetimes in .NET Core: Transient, Scoped, Singleton.
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

The DI container decides how long a resolved instance lives, based on the lifetime it was registered with. .NET Core defines three: Transient (a new instance every time), Scoped (one instance per DI scope — per HTTP request in a web app), and Singleton (one instance for the whole application lifetime).

✅ Advantages

  • Transient — zero shared state between callers; safest default for cheap, stateless helpers
  • Scoped — matches the natural unit of work of a web request; ideal for DbContext and repositories that must share one change tracker
  • Singleton — avoids repeated construction cost; perfect for caches and read-only configuration shared across all requests
  • Choosing the right lifetime prevents subtle bugs like stale data, thread-safety violations, and memory growth

💻 Examples

// Transient — new instance every resolution
builder.Services.AddTransient<IPricingCalculator, PricingCalculator>();

// Scoped — one per HTTP request
builder.Services.AddScoped<IAuthService, AuthService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<DashboardService>();

// Singleton — one for the whole app
builder.Services.AddSingleton<FundHoldingsService>();

// Worker Service (no HTTP scope) — everything is Singleton
services.AddSingleton<PaymentReminderService>();
services.AddSingleton<IConfigEmailSMTPDataService, ConfigEmailSMTPDataService>();

🎯 Uses

  • Transient — lightweight stateless services, e.g. calculators, mappers, validators
  • Scoped — DbContext, repositories, unit-of-work services, anything tied to one request
  • Singleton — in-memory caches, IHttpClientFactory-managed clients, read-only configuration wrappers
  • Worker Services / background jobs, where there's no HTTP request scope, so almost everything defaults to Singleton

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Transient creates a brand-new instance every time it's requested — best for lightweight, stateless services with no shared state. Scoped creates one instance per DI scope, which in a web app means one per HTTP request — everything in that request shares the same instance, which is exactly what DbContext needs for consistent change tracking. Singleton creates one instance for the entire application lifetime, shared across all requests and threads, so it must be thread-safe — I use it for caches and configuration. My rule of thumb: start with Scoped, use Singleton only for stateless or cacheable services, and reserve Transient for cheap, stateless helpers where a fresh instance per call is actually required.

projectExample.explanation: FolioTrack uses Scoped for most services — one instance per HTTP request is natural for web APIs. FundHoldingsService is Singleton because it caches expensive API data across all requests. In PaymentReminder (a Worker Service), there's no concept of an HTTP request scope, so everything is Singleton.

followUps.question: Why is Singleton risky for SqlConnection or DbContext?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

DbContext and SqlConnection are stateful and not thread-safe. Registering either as Singleton forces every concurrent request to share the same instance, which conflicts directly with what they're designed for — a single unit of work.

✅ Advantages

  • Correctly scoping these types avoids race conditions when multiple requests read/write the same change tracker
  • Prevents unbounded memory growth from EF Core's change tracker accumulating entities across the app's entire lifetime
  • Keeps data fresh — a new DbContext per request means every request re-queries instead of seeing stale cached entities
  • Lets the connection pool underneath do its job of safely reusing physical connections

💻 Examples

// ❌ Never do this
builder.Services.AddSingleton<AppDbContext>();

// ✅ Always Scoped — AddDbContext registers Scoped by default
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(options =>
    options.UseSqlServer(connectionString));

🎯 Uses

  • Registering EF Core's DbContext (always via AddDbContext, which is Scoped by default)
  • Registering raw SqlConnection-based repositories that must not be shared across concurrent requests
  • Diagnosing production bugs where data looks stale or corrupted under load — a captured Singleton DbContext is a common root cause

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Both carry stateful, non-thread-safe context that must be scoped to one unit of work. As a Singleton, DbContext's change tracker keeps accumulating every entity ever loaded across all requests — that's a memory leak and it slows every query down. Worse, concurrent requests would mutate the same change tracker at once, causing data corruption or exceptions, and the connection would be held open for the app's entire lifetime instead of being returned to the pool. SqlConnection has the same problem — it can only run one command at a time, so concurrent requests would block each other. That's why AddDbContext registers Scoped by default, and I never override that.

followUps.question: When would you use Transient for a repository?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Transient repositories are uncommon but valid when a repository is genuinely stateless (no shared DbContext) or when you need complete isolation between operations, so that a new instance is created on every resolution.

✅ Advantages

  • Guarantees callers never accidentally share mutable state, even within the same request
  • Works well for stateless, HTTP/file-based repositories that don't wrap DbContext
  • Cheap to construct, so the overhead of creating a new instance per call is negligible

💻 Examples

// Reasonable Transient — stateless, no shared DbContext needed
builder.Services.AddTransient<ICurrencyRateProvider, FxApiProvider>();

// Bad Transient — repositories wrapping DbContext get DIFFERENT contexts
builder.Services.AddTransient<IInvoiceRepository, EfInvoiceRepository>();
builder.Services.AddTransient<IPaymentRepository, EfPaymentRepository>();
// These won't share a transaction — SaveChanges on one won't include the other

🎯 Uses

  • Stateless, HTTP-based, or file-based repository wrappers with no shared change tracker
  • Batch-processing steps where each item must start with a completely fresh state
  • Never for repositories that wrap EF Core's DbContext — those must be Scoped to share one Unit of Work

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Almost never for a repository backed by DbContext — Scoped is correct there because you want every repository in the same request to share one change tracker and commit together in one SaveChangesAsync(). Transient makes sense only when the repository is stateless, like a pure HTTP or file wrapper with no shared context, or when you deliberately want isolation between operations within the same request, such as a batch job where each item must not see another item's pending changes. My rule: if it wraps DbContext, it's Scoped; if it's a pure I/O wrapper with no shared state, Transient is fine.

questions.tip: Rule of thumb: DbContext → Scoped, Repository → Scoped, HttpClient → Singleton via IHttpClientFactory, Stateless utility → Transient or Singleton, In-memory cache → Singleton. Worker Services use all Singletons because there's no HTTP request scope.

questions.question: What is captive dependency? How do you safely inject a Scoped service into a Singleton?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

A captive dependency happens when a longer-lived service (Singleton) holds a reference to a shorter-lived one (Scoped or Transient). The Scoped service is resolved once, when the Singleton is first constructed, and then held for the app's entire lifetime — effectively becoming a Singleton itself and breaking its intended contract.

✅ Advantages

  • Understanding this anti-pattern helps you avoid stale EF Core change-tracker state and shared mutable state leaking across unrelated requests
  • ASP.NET Core's container can detect and throw on this at Development time (or startup, with ValidateOnBuild), catching the bug before it reaches production
  • The fix (IServiceScopeFactory) gives you an explicit, controlled Unit-of-Work boundary instead of an implicit, accidental one

💻 Examples

Injecting AppDbContext (Scoped) directly into a Singleton captures it forever:

// ❌ Captive dependency — Singleton captures Scoped DbContext
public class ReportCache  // registered as Singleton
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _db;  // Scoped — DANGEROUS!
    public ReportCache(AppDbContext db) => _db = db;
}

// ✅ Correct — use IServiceScopeFactory to create a scope on demand
public class ReportCache  // Singleton
{
    private readonly IServiceScopeFactory _scopeFactory;
    public ReportCache(IServiceScopeFactory sf) => _scopeFactory = sf;

    public async Task RefreshAsync()
    {
        using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
        // db is properly scoped and disposed with the scope
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Any BackgroundService / IHostedService that needs DbContext or another Scoped service
  • Singleton caches or schedulers that periodically need fresh, request-like access to Scoped data
  • Diagnosing production incidents where data from one request seems to leak into another

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Captive dependency is when a longer-lived service captures a shorter-lived one — typically a Singleton holding a Scoped DbContext, which then lives for the whole app instead of one request. That causes stale change-tracker state, memory growth, and data leaking between requests because everyone shares the same instance. ASP.NET Core's container throws an InvalidOperationException in Development mode when this is detected. The safe fix is to inject IServiceScopeFactory into the Singleton and call CreateScope() to resolve the Scoped service fresh, inside a using block, per operation — this is the standard pattern for BackgroundServices that need DbContext.

projectExample.explanation: BackgroundService is registered as Singleton. IReminderRepository uses DbContext which must be Scoped. We inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a new scope on each iteration — this gives a fresh DbContext per execution cycle, preventing stale EF Core change tracker state.

followUps.question: What error do you get when captive dependency is detected?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

The built-in container throws a descriptive InvalidOperationException the moment the Singleton is first resolved and it tries to pull in the Scoped service — but only when scope validation is enabled.

✅ Advantages

  • The message names both the offending Scoped service and the Singleton consuming it, so diagnosis is immediate
  • ValidateOnBuild = true moves the failure to app startup instead of the first incoming request
  • Failing fast at startup (rather than silently in Production) is far cheaper than debugging a data-leak incident later

💻 Examples

// Exact error:
// System.InvalidOperationException:
// Cannot consume scoped service 'MyApp.Data.AppDbContext'
// from singleton 'MyApp.Services.ReportCacheService'.

// Enable validation in ALL environments, not just Development
builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(options =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes = true;   // detects captive dependencies
    options.ValidateOnBuild = true;  // throws at startup, not first request
});

🎯 Uses

  • Catching captive dependencies during local development before code review
  • Hardening CI/CD by enabling ValidateOnBuild so the app refuses to start with a broken dependency graph
  • Explaining, in an interview, exactly what the runtime error looks like — it's a strong signal you've hit this in real code

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

You get InvalidOperationException: Cannot consume scoped service '{ServiceType}' from singleton '{SingletonType}'. By default this only fires in Development (scope validation is off in Production), so the dangerous behavior can slip through silently unless you explicitly enable ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild in all environments. I always turn both on so the app fails fast at startup instead of leaking state in production.

followUps.question: Can you disable the captive dependency check? Should you?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Yes — setting ValidateScopes = false turns off the runtime check. But you should almost never do it, because the check exists specifically to catch a bug class that's extremely hard to debug once it reaches production.

✅ Advantages

  • Keeping validation on costs nothing at runtime and catches a real class of production bugs early
  • Disabling it only hides the symptom — the captive dependency and its side effects (stale data, leaks) still happen
  • The one legitimate exception is incrementally migrating a large legacy codebase where dependencies are being fixed piece by piece

💻 Examples

// How to disable (rarely justified)
builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(options =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes = false;
});

🎯 Uses

  • Legacy codebase migrations where captive dependencies are being fixed incrementally and validation would block every build
  • Should not be used to silence the error for otherwise-shippable new code — fix the dependency graph instead

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

You can, but I wouldn't unless I'm migrating a large legacy codebase incrementally. The check exists to catch bugs that are very hard to debug in production — data leaking between requests is a real correctness and security concern, not just an annoyance. Treat the validation error like a compiler error: fix the actual lifetime mismatch rather than turning off the safety net.

followUps.question: How does this pattern relate to the Unit of Work pattern?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() effectively creates a new Unit of Work boundary on demand. Each scope gets its own DbContext with a fresh change tracker, which is exactly what EF Core's Unit of Work implementation is.

✅ Advantages

  • Groups all the operations inside one scope into a single logical transaction, committed with one SaveChangesAsync()
  • Mirrors how ASP.NET Core already works for web requests — one scope per request equals one Unit of Work per request
  • Lets BackgroundServices replicate that same guarantee manually, one scope per execution cycle

💻 Examples

// Both repositories share the SAME DbContext (Scoped) inside one Unit of Work
public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository orderRepo,
    IInventoryRepository inventoryRepo,
    AppDbContext db)
{
    public async Task PlaceOrderAsync(CreateOrderRequest req)
    {
        await orderRepo.AddAsync(new Order(req));
        await inventoryRepo.DecrementStockAsync(req.ProductId, req.Quantity);

        // Single transaction — both or neither
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Designing transactional boundaries in web APIs (one request = one scope = one Unit of Work)
  • Designing transactional boundaries in BackgroundServices via manually created scopes
  • Explaining why EF Core's DbContext should be Scoped — it's what makes it behave as a Unit of Work

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Unit of Work groups multiple database operations so they succeed or fail together, and in EF Core, DbContext is the Unit of Work — it tracks changes and commits them atomically via SaveChangesAsync(). The Scoped lifetime is what makes this work correctly: all repositories in the same request or scope share the same DbContext, so one SaveChangesAsync() call commits everything together. When I call _scopeFactory.CreateScope() inside a Singleton, I'm manually creating a new Unit of Work boundary for that execution cycle — the scope boundary literally is the Unit of Work boundary.

questions.tip: Any time you have a BackgroundService that needs DbContext, use IServiceScopeFactory. This comes up in almost every interview for Worker Service / background job experience.

questions.question: What is the difference between IServiceCollection.Add() vs TryAdd()? What about AddScoped vs AddKeyedScoped?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Add*() always registers a service, even if it's already registered — the last registration wins for single-service resolution, but all registrations show up when injecting IEnumerable<T>. TryAdd*() registers only if no registration for that service type exists yet, which is safe for extension methods that shouldn't override a caller's own registration. .NET 8's keyed services (AddKeyedScoped<T>(key)) let you register multiple implementations of the same interface under different keys and resolve a specific one with [FromKeyedServices(key)].

✅ Advantages

  • TryAdd*() makes library/extension code idempotent — calling AddMyLibrary() twice doesn't duplicate registrations
  • Keyed services solve the "multiple implementations of one interface" problem natively, without a custom factory
  • Avoids the older workaround of injecting IEnumerable<T> and filtering at runtime just to pick one implementation

💻 Examples

// TryAdd — safe registration that won't override an existing one
services.TryAddSingleton<IHttpClientFactory, DefaultHttpClientFactory>();

// .NET 8 Keyed services
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IEmailService, GmailService>("gmail");
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IEmailService, SmtpService>("smtp");

// Inject a specific implementation
public class NotificationService(
    [FromKeyedServices("smtp")] IEmailService emailService) { }

🎯 Uses

  • Writing reusable IServiceCollection extension methods (AddXyz()) that shouldn't clobber a caller's own registration
  • Registering multiple providers of the same interface (e.g. Gmail vs SMTP, multiple payment gateways) and selecting one explicitly at the injection site
  • Framework/infrastructure code, where ASP.NET Core itself uses TryAdd* extensively so calling AddMvc() twice is safe

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Add* always registers, so calling it twice for the same type produces two registrations — the last one wins when you inject the type directly, but both appear in IEnumerable<T>. TryAdd* only registers if nothing is already registered for that service type, which is what you want in library code so you don't stomp on a consumer's own registration. Before .NET 8 I'd inject IEnumerable<T> to handle multiple implementations of one interface; now keyed services let me register AddKeyedScoped<IEmailService, GmailService>("gmail") and ...SmtpService>("smtp"), then pull a specific one with [FromKeyedServices("smtp")] — much cleaner than the factory-function workarounds we used to write.

projectExample.explanation: TryAdd is important when writing library code. Keyed services solve the 'multiple implementations of one interface' problem without needing factory patterns.

followUps.question: How do you inject multiple implementations of the same interface (without keyed services)?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Register each implementation separately against the same interface, then inject IEnumerable<T> — the container hands back every registered implementation as a collection, in registration order.

✅ Advantages

  • Works on every .NET version, no need for .NET 8's keyed services
  • Natural fit for the Strategy or Chain-of-Responsibility pattern — iterate and pick, or run all of them
  • No extra registration ceremony beyond normal AddScoped<TInterface, TImpl>() calls

💻 Examples

builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationChannel, EmailChannel>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationChannel, SmsChannel>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationChannel, PushChannel>();

public class NotificationService(IEnumerable<INotificationChannel> channels)
{
    public async Task NotifyAllAsync(string message)
    {
        foreach (var channel in channels)
            await channel.SendAsync(message);
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Fan-out scenarios — notify via every registered channel (email + SMS + push)
  • Strategy selection — filter IEnumerable<T> by a discriminator property to pick the right implementation at runtime
  • Pre-.NET-8 codebases where keyed services aren't available

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Register every implementation against the same interface with separate AddScoped<IService, ImplX>() calls, then inject IEnumerable<IService> in the consumer — the container resolves all registrations as a collection. That's how I implemented the Strategy pattern with DI before keyed services existed: inject IEnumerable<IPaymentStrategy> and pick the right one at runtime with something like strategies.First(s => s.Name == provider). With .NET 8, keyed services are cleaner when you only ever need one specific implementation resolved by key, but IEnumerable<T> is still the right tool when you genuinely need all of them, like broadcasting a notification to every channel.

followUps.question: What is TryAddEnumerable and when do you use it?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

TryAddEnumerable adds a service to the IEnumerable<T> collection only if that exact implementation type isn't already registered for the service type — unlike TryAdd, which checks the service type only.

✅ Advantages

  • Prevents the same concrete implementation from being registered twice in a collection, while still allowing different implementations to coexist
  • Makes extension methods idempotent even when they register multiple implementations of the same interface
  • Used extensively inside ASP.NET Core itself so calling framework setup methods more than once doesn't duplicate validators/handlers

💻 Examples

// TryAddEnumerable: adds only if this specific implementation isn't registered
services.TryAddEnumerable(
    ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IValidator, EmailValidator>());
services.TryAddEnumerable(
    ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IValidator, PhoneValidator>());  // added — different type
services.TryAddEnumerable(
    ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IValidator, EmailValidator>());  // no-op — already registered

🎯 Uses

  • Library/extension-method authors calling AddXyz() multiple times without wanting duplicate registrations
  • Framework and infrastructure code — application code rarely needs it directly

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

TryAddEnumerable adds a service to the IEnumerable<T> collection only if the exact same implementation type isn't already registered for that service type — it prevents duplicate registrations while still letting multiple different implementations coexist. It's more specific than TryAdd, which only checks the service type. The main use case is library and framework authors: ASP.NET Core itself uses it internally so calling setup methods like AddMvc() more than once doesn't register the same validators or conventions twice. Application code rarely needs it — it's mainly for infrastructure code that might run its setup logic more than once.

questions.tip: Keyed services (AddKeyedScoped) were added in .NET 8 — a great answer if the interviewer asks about new .NET 8 DI features.

questions.question: How does property injection work in .NET Core? Why is constructor injection preferred?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

The built-in .NET DI container does not support property injection out of the box — it only performs constructor injection. Property injection requires a third-party container like Autofac or Castle Windsor. Constructor injection is the only first-class option in ASP.NET Core, and it's also the recommended one.

✅ Advantages

  • Dependencies are explicit and required — the object literally cannot be constructed without them
  • Immutable once set — assigned in the constructor and never reassigned
  • Easier to unit test — every dependency is visible in the constructor signature
  • Fails fast — a missing dependency throws at startup/construction, not silently at some later runtime call

💻 Examples

// Constructor injection — preferred approach
public class DashboardController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly DashboardService _dashboardService;
    private readonly ILogger<DashboardController> _logger;

    public DashboardController(
        DashboardService dashboardService,
        ILogger<DashboardController> logger)
    {
        _dashboardService = dashboardService;
        _logger = logger;
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Every controller, service, and repository in an ASP.NET Core app — the default and expected pattern
  • Required dependencies that a class cannot function without
  • Never for genuinely optional dependencies — those are better modeled as nullable constructor parameters with a documented default, not properties set after construction

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

The built-in .NET container only supports constructor injection — property injection needs a third-party container and even then I'd avoid it. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and required: the object can't exist without them, they're immutable once assigned, and every dependency is visible just by reading the constructor signature, which makes unit testing straightforward. It also fails fast — a missing registration throws at startup during the DI container's validation, not silently at runtime when some code path finally touches a null property. Property injection, by contrast, creates optional-looking dependencies that can be forgotten and cause NullReferenceExceptions much later.

projectExample.explanation: Every controller in FolioTrack uses constructor injection. Missing services would cause an exception at startup during DI container validation, not silently fail at runtime.

followUps.question: What happens if you have too many constructor parameters?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Too many constructor parameters (generally more than 4–5) is a code smell that usually means the class is doing too much and violating the Single Responsibility Principle.

✅ Advantages

  • Instant, objective SRP health check — you don't need a code review to spot it, just count the parameters
  • Prompts extracting a cohesive orchestration service, which improves readability and testability of both the extracted class and the original one
  • Prevents controllers/services from silently accumulating unrelated responsibilities over time

💻 Examples

// ❌ Constructor over-injection — 7 parameters is too many
public class ReportController(
    IUserRepository userRepo, IInvoiceRepository invoiceRepo,
    IPaymentRepository paymentRepo, IEmailService emailSvc,
    IPdfService pdfSvc, ILogger<ReportController> logger, IMapper mapper)
{ }

// ✅ Refactored — extract a cohesive ReportService
public class ReportController(IReportService reportSvc, ILogger<ReportController> logger)
{ }

public class ReportService(
    IUserRepository userRepo, IInvoiceRepository invoiceRepo,
    IPaymentRepository paymentRepo, IPdfService pdfSvc)
{ }

🎯 Uses

  • Code review heuristic — flag classes with 5+ constructor dependencies for a possible split
  • Refactoring bloated controllers by extracting an orchestrating application service
  • Legitimate exception: true orchestrators (e.g. a CheckoutService coordinating inventory, payment, and email) may need more — use judgment

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

More than 4–5 constructor parameters is a strong signal the class is violating the Single Responsibility Principle and doing too many things. The fix is usually to extract a cohesive service that groups the related dependencies — for example, pulling several repository dependencies out of a controller into a dedicated ReportService. I mention this as self-awareness in interviews: if I see a constructor growing past 5 parameters, that's my cue to stop and ask whether the class needs to be split, rather than just adding another parameter.

questions.tip: Interviewer tip: If a class has more than 4–5 constructor parameters, it's usually a sign that the class has too many responsibilities — it should be split (SRP). Mention this as self-awareness.

questions.question: What is IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, and IOptionsMonitor<T>? When do you use each?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

These are .NET's typed configuration options pattern — strongly-typed, DI-friendly access to appsettings.json values, avoiding magic strings like Configuration["Jwt:Key"] scattered across the codebase.

✅ Advantages

  • IOptions<T> (Singleton) — reads config once at startup; cheapest option, safe to inject anywhere including Singletons
  • IOptionsSnapshot<T> (Scoped) — recomputed per request/scope, supports hot-reload of appsettings.json
  • IOptionsMonitor<T> (Singleton) — live-updating with an OnChange callback, usable inside Singletons that need current config without restarting
  • Type safety catches config typos and shape mismatches at bind time instead of at first use

💻 Examples

// Register options
builder.Services.Configure<JwtSettings>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("JwtSettings"));
builder.Services.Configure<SmtpSettings>(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Smtp"));

// appsettings.json
// { "JwtSettings": { "Key": "...", "Issuer": "...", "ExpiryDays": 7 } }

// Inject in a service
public class JwtHelper(IOptions<JwtSettings> options)
{
    private readonly JwtSettings _settings = options.Value;
}

🎯 Uses

  • IOptions<T> — config that never changes after startup, e.g. JWT settings, SMTP settings
  • IOptionsSnapshot<T> — per-request config that should reflect an appsettings.json edit without restarting, e.g. feature toggles read once per request
  • IOptionsMonitor<T> — Singleton services (caches, background workers) that need to react live to config changes via OnChange

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

All three give strongly-typed access to configuration, but differ in lifetime and refresh behavior. IOptions<T> is Singleton and reads config once at startup — simplest, and safe to inject into Singletons. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is Scoped and recomputes per request, so it picks up hot-reloaded config, but that also means it can't be injected into a Singleton without becoming a captive dependency. IOptionsMonitor<T> is Singleton but stays live — it exposes CurrentValue and an OnChange callback, so I use it when a Singleton itself needs to react to config changes without an app restart. Both of our projects use IOptions<T> for JWT and SMTP settings because that config genuinely doesn't need to change at runtime.

projectExample.explanation: Both projects use IOptions<T> for JWT and SMTP config — startup configuration that doesn't need runtime updates. IOptionsMonitor would be overkill here. The key benefit: no magic strings for config keys, type safety, easy unit testing with fake options.

followUps.question: How do you validate IOptions<T> at startup, including with DataAnnotations?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

By default, options config is read lazily — a missing or invalid value only throws when code calls options.Value. Startup validation makes the app refuse to start if configuration is invalid, using either DataAnnotation attributes on the options class or custom validation logic.

✅ Advantages

  • Fails at dotnet run instead of at 2am when a customer's request first hits the broken config path
  • [Required], [Range], [MinLength] etc. reuse the same validation attributes as ASP.NET Core model binding — no new API to learn
  • Custom .Validate() or IValidateOptions<T> covers cross-property rules DataAnnotations can't express

💻 Examples

public class JwtSettings
{
    [Required, MinLength(32)]
    public string Key { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    [Range(1, 365)]
    public int ExpiryDays { get; set; } = 7;
}

builder.Services.AddOptions<JwtSettings>()
    .BindConfiguration("JwtSettings")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()   // runs [Required], [Range], etc.
    .ValidateOnStart();          // throws at startup, not first access

// Custom validation
builder.Services.AddOptions<SmtpSettings>()
    .BindConfiguration("Smtp")
    .Validate(smtp => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(smtp.Host) && smtp.Port is >= 1 and <= 65535,
        "SMTP settings are invalid — check Host and Port")
    .ValidateOnStart();

🎯 Uses

  • Any config class backing secrets, connection info, or thresholds where a missing value should hard-fail deployment
  • CI/CD pipelines — a bad config value fails the deploy immediately instead of surfacing as a production incident
  • Enforcing invariants across multiple properties via a custom IValidateOptions<T> implementation

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

I chain .AddOptions<T>().BindConfiguration("Section").ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart(). ValidateDataAnnotations() enforces attributes like [Required] and [Range] on the options class, and ValidateOnStart() forces that validation to run at app startup rather than lazily on first access, so the app fails immediately with a clear OptionsValidationException listing every invalid field. For rules that DataAnnotations can't express — like cross-field checks — I use a custom .Validate() predicate or an IValidateOptions<T> implementation. The payoff is catching a missing JWT key or bad SMTP port during dotnet run, not as a NullReferenceException deep in production.

questions.tip: Mention builder.Services.AddOptions().ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() for startup validation — it catches missing config immediately instead of at runtime.

questions.question: How do you register open generic types in .NET DI, override them for a specific type, and mix the two?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Open generic registration lets you register a generic service without specifying its type parameter — the container fills it in at resolution time. Syntax: services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(GenericRepository<>)). When you inject IRepository<Product>, the container builds a GenericRepository<Product> automatically — the basis of the generic repository pattern.

✅ Advantages

  • One registration handles every entity type, eliminating per-entity boilerplate registrations
  • Closed generic registrations (for a specific T) can be layered on top and take priority, so you keep the generic default while overriding special cases
  • Very common in enterprise codebases — recognizing and using it signals familiarity with advanced DI beyond the basics

💻 Examples

// Open generic — handles all T by default
builder.Services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfCoreRepository<>));

public interface IRepository<T> where T : class
{
    Task<T?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
    Task<IEnumerable<T>> GetAllAsync();
}

public class EfCoreRepository<T>(AppDbContext db) : IRepository<T> where T : class
{
    private readonly DbSet<T> _set = db.Set<T>();
    public async Task<T?> GetByIdAsync(int id) => await _set.FindAsync(id);
    public async Task<IEnumerable<T>> GetAllAsync() => await _set.ToListAsync();
}

// Override for a specific type — closed generic registered AFTER the open one wins
builder.Services.AddScoped<IRepository<Order>, CachedOrderRepository>();

// IRepository<Product> → EfCoreRepository<Product>  (open generic)
// IRepository<Order>   → CachedOrderRepository       (specific override)

🎯 Uses

  • Generic repository pattern — one IRepository<T> registration for every EF Core entity
  • Cross-cutting decorators/handlers over generic pipelines, e.g. IRequestHandler<,> in a mediator pattern
  • Overriding the generic default for one entity that needs special behavior — caching, auditing, or custom queries — without touching the rest

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Open generic registration — services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfCoreRepository<>)) — lets the container build a closed generic like EfCoreRepository<Product> automatically whenever IRepository<Product> is requested, so I don't need a registration per entity. If one entity needs special behavior — say Order needs caching or auditing — I register a specific closed generic, services.AddScoped<IRepository<Order>, CachedOrderRepository>(), after the open generic. The container prefers the more specific closed-generic registration, so IRepository<Order> resolves to CachedOrderRepository while every other entity still falls back to the generic implementation. Open and closed generics coexist cleanly this way, which is exactly the pattern behind mediator-style pipelines like IRequestHandler<,> too.

projectExample.explanation: One registration handles all entity types. InvestmentController can inject IRepository<Investment>, UserController can inject IRepository<User> — both resolved automatically without separate registrations.

questions.tip: This pattern is common in enterprise codebases. If you've used it, say so — it shows you understand advanced DI patterns beyond the basics.

questions.question: What is IHttpClientFactory and why should you always use it instead of new HttpClient()?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Creating new HttpClient() per call causes socket exhaustion — each instance holds a socket in TCP TIME_WAIT even after disposal, eventually exhausting available ports under load. IHttpClientFactory manages a pool of HttpMessageHandlers, reusing connections while rotating them periodically (default 2 minutes), and integrates with DI and Polly for retry/circuit-breaker policies.

✅ Advantages

  • Eliminates socket exhaustion by pooling and reusing handlers instead of creating a new socket per request
  • Avoids the opposite failure mode too — a single static HttpClient caches DNS forever, so it misses server IP changes; handler rotation fixes that
  • Integrates natively with DI (AddHttpClient<T>()) and with Polly for retries, circuit breakers, and timeouts

💻 Examples

// Typed client registration
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MfApiService>(client =>
{
    client.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.mfapi.in/");
    client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
});

// Named client
builder.Services.AddHttpClient("OdooClient", client =>
{
    client.BaseAddress = new Uri(config["OdooBaseUrl"]);
});

// Inject typed client
public class MfApiService(HttpClient httpClient) { }

// Inject named client via factory
public class OdooService(IHttpClientFactory factory)
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client = factory.CreateClient("OdooClient");
}

🎯 Uses

  • Any outbound HTTP call to a third-party or internal API — always via a typed or named client, never new HttpClient()
  • Adding resilience (retry, circuit breaker) with Polly or AddStandardResilienceHandler() around an external dependency
  • Diagnosing and fixing socket-exhaustion incidents in production caused by ad-hoc HttpClient instantiation in loops

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

new HttpClient() per request causes socket exhaustion — the underlying socket stays in TIME_WAIT after disposal, and under load you run out of ports. IHttpClientFactory fixes this by pooling HttpMessageHandlers and rotating them on a timer, by default every 2 minutes, so connections are reused within that window but DNS doesn't go stale. I always register clients via AddHttpClient<TService>() for a typed client or AddHttpClient("name", ...) for a named one, and it also plugs directly into Polly for retry and circuit-breaker policies. In CSInvoice we originally called new HttpClient() inside a loop, which caused real socket exhaustion under load; switching to IHttpClientFactory with a typed client fixed it.

projectExample.explanation: CSInvoice originally used 'new HttpClient()' inside loops — this caused socket exhaustion under load. Fixed by switching to IHttpClientFactory with typed clients. FolioTrack uses AddHttpClient<MfApiService>() for the mutual fund API calls — cleaner and properly pooled.

followUps.question: How do you add Polly retry and circuit-breaker policies to IHttpClientFactory?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Polly is a .NET resilience library providing retry, circuit-breaker, timeout, and bulkhead policies. It attaches directly to a registered client via .AddPolicyHandler(), or in .NET 8+ via the built-in AddStandardResilienceHandler().

✅ Advantages

  • Transient HTTP failures (5xx, timeouts) get retried automatically with exponential backoff instead of failing the whole request
  • Circuit breakers stop hammering a struggling downstream service, giving it time to recover
  • .NET 8's Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience package bundles retry + circuit breaker + timeout with one call

💻 Examples

var retryPolicy = HttpPolicyExtensions
    .HandleTransientHttpError()
    .WaitAndRetryAsync(3, attempt => TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Math.Pow(2, attempt)));

var circuitBreakerPolicy = HttpPolicyExtensions
    .HandleTransientHttpError()
    .CircuitBreakerAsync(5, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MfApiService>(client =>
    client.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.mfapi.in/"))
    .AddPolicyHandler(retryPolicy)
    .AddPolicyHandler(circuitBreakerPolicy);

// .NET 8 — built-in bundle
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MfApiService>()
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler();

🎯 Uses

  • Calling flaky third-party APIs (payment gateways, market data feeds) where transient failures are expected
  • Protecting a struggling downstream dependency from being overwhelmed by retries via a circuit breaker
  • .NET 8 projects — prefer AddStandardResilienceHandler() over hand-rolled Polly policies unless you need custom behavior

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Polly plugs into IHttpClientFactory via .AddPolicyHandler() on the registered client. I typically add a retry policy with exponential backoff for transient errors (HandleTransientHttpError() covers 5xx and network exceptions) and a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency for a cool-down window. In .NET 8, Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience's AddStandardResilienceHandler() gives you retry, circuit breaker, and timeout out of the box with one line, which is what I'd default to unless the project needs a custom policy.

followUps.question: What is the difference between typed, named, and basic HttpClient registrations?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

IHttpClientFactory supports three consumption patterns: typed clients (a service class receives a pre-configured HttpClient directly), named clients (resolved by string key via the factory), and basic clients (an unconfigured client from factory.CreateClient()).

✅ Advantages

  • Typed clients are the most DI-idiomatic — all HTTP logic for one external API lives in one testable class
  • Named clients let multiple services share the same pre-configured client without a dedicated wrapper class
  • Basic clients cover ad-hoc, dynamic-endpoint scenarios where a dedicated typed client would be overkill

💻 Examples

// Typed — cleanest, most DI-idiomatic
services.AddHttpClient<GitHubService>(c =>
    c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.github.com/"));
public class GitHubService(HttpClient client)
{
    public Task<string> GetUserAsync(string u) => client.GetStringAsync($"/users/{u}");
}

// Named — pre-configured, referenced by string
services.AddHttpClient("GitHub", c => c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.github.com/"));
var client = factory.CreateClient("GitHub");

// Basic — unconfigured, ad-hoc
services.AddHttpClient();
var client2 = factory.CreateClient();

🎯 Uses

  • Typed — a dedicated service class per external API (default choice)
  • Named — the same configured client needed from several unrelated services
  • Basic — dynamic or one-off requests where the endpoint isn't known ahead of time

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Typed clients register a service class that receives HttpClient directly in its constructor via AddHttpClient<TService>() — the cleanest option, since all the HTTP logic for one API is encapsulated and easy to mock in tests. Named clients are registered with a string key and resolved via factory.CreateClient("name"), useful when several services need the same pre-configured client without wrapping it in a dedicated class. Basic clients just call factory.CreateClient() for an unconfigured client, which I only use for genuinely ad-hoc requests. I default to typed clients — they're testable, avoid magic strings, and keep each external API's concerns in one place.

followUps.question: What is handler lifetime and why does it matter?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Handler lifetime is how long the underlying HttpMessageHandler (which owns the actual socket/connection) lives before IHttpClientFactory rotates it out — 2 minutes by default. This is the mechanism that prevents both socket exhaustion and DNS staleness at the same time.

✅ Advantages

  • Short enough that DNS changes (e.g. a failover to a new server IP) are picked up promptly
  • Long enough to amortize the cost of establishing new connections under normal load
  • Old handlers aren't disposed immediately — in-flight requests finish first, so rotation is safe under load

💻 Examples

// Configure handler lifetime per named/typed client
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MfApiService>()
    .SetHandlerLifetime(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));

// Rule: never dispose a factory-created HttpClient yourself —
// the factory/handler manages the socket lifecycle, not the client wrapper

🎯 Uses

  • Services calling APIs behind a load balancer or DNS-based failover, where stale DNS would route to a dead server
  • Tuning connection reuse vs. failover responsiveness for high-throughput integrations

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Handler lifetime is how long IHttpClientFactory keeps reusing the same underlying HttpMessageHandler before creating a fresh one — 2 minutes by default. This solves two opposite problems at once: creating a brand-new handler (and socket) per call causes socket exhaustion, while a single handler that lives forever caches DNS lookups forever and misses IP changes. Rotating every couple of minutes keeps connections reused in the short term while still picking up DNS changes reasonably quickly. It's configurable per client with .SetHandlerLifetime(), and importantly, you should never dispose a factory-created HttpClient yourself — the handler underneath is what actually owns the socket.

questions.tip: Mentioning CSInvoice's socket exhaustion bug and fix is a great real-world story for this question. Always use IHttpClientFactory or AddHttpClient<T>() — never new HttpClient() inside a class.

questions.question: What is the service locator pattern? Why is it considered an anti-pattern, and when is IServiceProvider acceptable?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

The service locator pattern is when a class calls IServiceProvider.GetService<T>() directly to resolve its own dependencies, instead of declaring them in the constructor. It's generally considered an anti-pattern in application code, though a few infrastructure scenarios genuinely need it.

✅ Advantages

  • Constructor injection keeps dependencies visible and explicit — you can tell what a class needs just by reading its signature
  • Testability — mocking a constructor parameter is trivial; mocking a global container is not
  • Fails fast — a missing registration throws at startup instead of deep inside a method at runtime
  • Respects the Dependency Inversion Principle — the class depends on its abstractions, not on the container itself

💻 Examples

// ❌ Anti-pattern — service locator, hidden dependency
public class ReportService(IServiceProvider sp)
{
    public void Generate()
    {
        var db = sp.GetService<AppDbContext>(); // hidden!
    }
}

// ✅ Correct — constructor injection, explicit dependency
public class ReportService(AppDbContext db)
{
    public void Generate() => db.Reports.ToList();
}

// ✅ Acceptable use — factory that must resolve a runtime-determined type
public class ExporterFactory(IServiceProvider sp)
{
    public IExporter Create(ExportFormat format) => format switch
    {
        ExportFormat.Excel => sp.GetRequiredService<ExcelExporter>(),
        ExportFormat.Pdf   => sp.GetRequiredService<PdfExporter>(),
        _ => throw new NotSupportedException()
    };
}

🎯 Uses

  • Avoid entirely in business logic, services, repositories, and controllers — always constructor-inject instead
  • Acceptable inside factory classes that resolve one of several implementations based on a runtime value
  • Acceptable inside Singleton middleware that needs a Scoped service — create a scope with sp.CreateScope() first
  • Acceptable in Program.cs bootstrapping code (running migrations, seeding data) before the app starts serving requests

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Service locator is when a class resolves its own dependencies at runtime via IServiceProvider.GetService<T>() instead of declaring them in its constructor. It's an anti-pattern because it hides dependencies — you have to read the method body to know what a class actually needs — and it breaks easy unit testing, since you can't just inject a mock. I avoid it everywhere in application code and stick to constructor injection. The exceptions where IServiceProvider is genuinely the right tool are narrow: factory classes that pick one of several implementations based on a runtime value, middleware that's registered as Singleton but needs a Scoped service (via sp.CreateScope()), and startup/bootstrapping code in Program.cs. Outside those, if I see IServiceProvider injected into a regular service, that's a design smell worth flagging in review.

projectExample.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit. If ReportService needs AppDbContext, that's immediately visible from the constructor. With service locator, a reviewer or tester has to read the entire method body to discover what the class actually needs.

followUps.question: When is using IServiceProvider directly acceptable?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

A handful of infrastructure-level scenarios legitimately need IServiceProvider because the type to resolve isn't known until runtime, or because a Singleton needs to reach a Scoped service.

✅ Advantages

  • Factory classes are still testable — you mock the factory interface, not the container
  • Middleware scope creation keeps Singleton middleware safe to use alongside Scoped services like DbContext
  • Confining IServiceProvider usage to a small number of well-understood infrastructure classes keeps the rest of the codebase clean

💻 Examples

// Middleware is Singleton — must create a scope manually for Scoped deps
public class RequestLoggingMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IServiceProvider sp)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext ctx)
    {
        using var scope = sp.CreateScope();
        var audit = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IAuditLogger>();
        await audit.LogAsync(ctx.Request.Path);
        await next(ctx);
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Abstract factories resolving a runtime-determined implementation
  • Singleton middleware/background workers needing a fresh Scoped service per operation
  • One-off startup/bootstrap code, e.g. resolving a seeding service before app.Run()

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

It's acceptable in factory methods that genuinely need to resolve an arbitrary type decided at runtime, in Singleton-scoped infrastructure like middleware that needs a Scoped service (via sp.CreateScope()), in BackgroundServices via IServiceScopeFactory, and in Program.cs bootstrapping code. In every one of those cases the container usage is contained to a small, well-known piece of infrastructure rather than spread through business logic. If I ever see IServiceProvider injected into a controller, repository, or domain service, that's the signal something should be refactored to constructor injection instead.

followUps.question: What is the difference between service locator and factory pattern?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Both resolve objects at runtime, but a factory exposes a specific, named creation contract that the consumer depends on, while service locator exposes the raw container itself — hiding what the consumer actually needs.

✅ Advantages

  • Factories are easy to mock — you fake the factory interface, not the whole DI container
  • Factories document intent through their interface name (IPaymentHandlerFactory tells you exactly what it creates)
  • Service locator hides that information entirely; you must read the implementation to know what's resolved

💻 Examples

// Service Locator — problematic, intent hidden
public class PaymentProcessor(IServiceProvider sp)
{
    public void Process(PaymentMethod method)
        => sp.GetService<IPaymentHandler>(); // what does this actually get?
}

// Factory Pattern — clean, explicit
public interface IPaymentHandlerFactory { IPaymentHandler Create(PaymentMethod method); }

public class PaymentProcessor(IPaymentHandlerFactory factory)
{
    public void Process(PaymentMethod method) => factory.Create(method);
}

// The factory implementation can use IServiceProvider internally — that's fine
public class PaymentHandlerFactory(IServiceProvider sp) : IPaymentHandlerFactory
{
    public IPaymentHandler Create(PaymentMethod method) => method switch
    {
        PaymentMethod.Card => sp.GetRequiredService<CardPaymentHandler>(),
        PaymentMethod.UPI  => sp.GetRequiredService<UpiPaymentHandler>(),
        _ => throw new NotSupportedException()
    };
}

🎯 Uses

  • Consumers that need to create one of several related objects based on a runtime discriminator
  • Wrapping unavoidable IServiceProvider usage behind a small, named, testable abstraction

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Factory pattern is about creating objects and is an accepted creational pattern in its own right; it doesn't inherently couple the consumer to a DI container. Service locator retrieves an existing registered service from a global registry, coupling the consumer directly to the container. A factory can use IServiceProvider internally to build its products, but from the consumer's point of view it just depends on a small, explicit factory interface — not on the container. That's the key distinction: PaymentProcessor depending on IPaymentHandlerFactory is clean and mockable; PaymentProcessor depending on IServiceProvider directly is the anti-pattern.

questions.tip: A great interview signal: say 'I avoid service locator in application code. It's only justified in factory methods or infrastructure-level code where types are determined at runtime.'

questions.question: How do you configure DI in a Worker Service (.NET BackgroundService)? How does it differ from Web API?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Worker Services use the same .NET Generic Host and DI container as Web APIs, just without ASP.NET Core's HTTP middleware pipeline. Because there's no incoming HTTP request, there's no automatic per-request scope — BackgroundService itself is registered as Singleton via AddHostedService, so its direct dependencies must be Singleton too, or resolved through IServiceScopeFactory.

✅ Advantages

  • No HTTP request scope means no free per-request DbContext the way Web API gets it — scopes must be created explicitly
  • Registering the hosted service is a one-liner (AddHostedService<T>()), and the Generic Host manages its start/stop lifecycle automatically
  • Same IServiceCollection API as Web API, so existing DI knowledge transfers directly — only the scoping story changes

💻 Examples

var host = Host.CreateDefaultBuilder(args)
    .ConfigureServices((ctx, services) =>
    {
        services.AddHostedService<PaymentReminderWorker>();

        // All Singleton (no HTTP scope in a worker)
        services.AddSingleton<IEmailService, SmtpEmailService>();

        // DbContext stays Scoped — accessed via IServiceScopeFactory
        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(opts =>
            opts.UseSqlServer(ctx.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
    })
    .Build();

await host.RunAsync();

🎯 Uses

  • Windows Services, Docker-hosted background jobs, and Azure WebJobs built on the Generic Host
  • Periodic tasks (reminders, invoice processing, cleanup jobs) that need DbContext via a manually created scope per cycle
  • Any long-running process where there's no HTTP pipeline but you still want the DI container's lifetime management

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Worker Services reuse the same Generic Host and DI container as Web API, but without ASP.NET Core middleware, so there's no automatic per-request scope. BackgroundService is registered Singleton via AddHostedService, so its dependencies are typically Singleton, and anything Scoped — most importantly DbContext — has to be resolved through IServiceScopeFactory inside ExecuteAsync, one scope per execution cycle. In PaymentReminder, which runs as a Windows Service / Docker container, IEmailService is Singleton since it's stateless and thread-safe, while DbContext stays Scoped and is resolved fresh on each loop iteration to avoid a stale EF Core change tracker. That's the key nuance interviewers look for — knowing Web API DI is not enough, you need to know Worker Services have no request scope at all.

projectExample.explanation: PaymentReminder runs as a Windows Service / Docker container. IEmailService is Singleton because it's stateless and thread-safe. DbContext is Scoped and accessed via IServiceScopeFactory inside ExecuteAsync — creating a new scope per execution cycle to avoid stale EF Core change tracker.

followUps.question: How do you stop a BackgroundService gracefully with CancellationToken?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

The stoppingToken passed into ExecuteAsync is triggered when the host receives a shutdown signal (Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, or IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()). Your code has to actively observe it — in the loop condition and in every awaited call — for shutdown to actually be graceful.

✅ Advantages

  • Passing the token into Task.Delay makes shutdown immediate instead of waiting out the full interval
  • Passing it into DB/HTTP calls lets in-flight work cancel cleanly instead of being abandoned mid-operation
  • Catching OperationCanceledException separately avoids logging expected shutdown as an error

💻 Examples

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        try
        {
            using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();
            var repo = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IReminderRepository>();
            await repo.ProcessDueRemindersAsync(stoppingToken);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) { break; } // expected on shutdown
        catch (Exception ex) { _logger.LogError(ex, "Error in worker cycle"); }

        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), stoppingToken);
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Any long-running BackgroundService that must stop cleanly during a deploy or container restart, without corrupting in-flight work
  • Configuring the host's shutdown timeout ("ShutdownTimeout": "00:00:30") so slow cleanup doesn't hang the process

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

The CancellationToken passed to ExecuteAsync fires when the host is asked to shut down. I pass it into every awaited call — Task.Delay, DB queries, HTTP calls — so those operations cancel immediately rather than finishing a full interval or hanging. I catch OperationCanceledException separately from other exceptions since it's the expected result of shutdown, not a bug, and let the loop exit cleanly. That combination is what makes a BackgroundService actually stop gracefully instead of being killed mid-operation.

followUps.question: What is the difference between IHostedService and BackgroundService?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

IHostedService is the interface with StartAsync/StopAsync that you implement fully yourself. BackgroundService is an abstract class implementing IHostedService that handles that plumbing for you and just asks you to implement ExecuteAsync, which it runs on a background Task.

✅ Advantages

  • BackgroundService removes almost all the lifecycle boilerplate for the common "long-running loop" case
  • IHostedService gives precise control when you need it — e.g. blocking startup until a cache is warmed before the app accepts traffic
  • Both integrate identically with the Generic Host's DI container and shutdown signaling

💻 Examples

// IHostedService — full control, useful for startup/shutdown work
public class DatabaseMigrator : IHostedService
{
    public async Task StartAsync(CancellationToken ct) => await ApplyMigrationsAsync(ct);
    public Task StopAsync(CancellationToken ct) => Task.CompletedTask;
}

// BackgroundService — for long-running background loops
public class InvoiceProcessor : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await ProcessBatchAsync(stoppingToken);
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • BackgroundService — the default choice for periodic/long-running jobs (reminders, queue processors)
  • IHostedService directly — startup-only tasks like running migrations or warming a cache before the app starts serving traffic

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

BackgroundService is an abstract base class implementing IHostedService that automatically runs your ExecuteAsync method on a background task and wires up the cancellation token for you — you only implement one method. IHostedService is the raw interface with StartAsync/StopAsync, giving full manual control over the lifecycle, which is useful for short, blocking startup work like running database migrations before the host finishes starting. For PaymentReminder-style periodic tasks I always extend BackgroundService — less boilerplate, and it already handles the background thread correctly.

followUps.question: How do you schedule a BackgroundService to run every N minutes?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

The simplest approach is await Task.Delay(interval, stoppingToken) at the end of the loop. For fixed cadence unaffected by processing time, use .NET 6+'s PeriodicTimer; for CRON-style scheduling, use Quartz.NET.

✅ Advantages

  • Task.Delay is trivial to write but drifts — the actual cycle time is delay + processing time
  • PeriodicTimer ticks on a fixed cadence regardless of how long the previous iteration took
  • Quartz.NET adds CRON expressions and missed-fire handling for genuinely complex schedules

💻 Examples

// PeriodicTimer (.NET 6+, preferred over Task.Delay)
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct))
    {
        await DoWorkAsync(ct);
    }
}

// Quartz.NET — CRON scheduling
builder.Services.AddQuartz(q =>
{
    var jobKey = new JobKey("InvoiceJob");
    q.AddJob<InvoiceProcessingJob>(o => o.WithIdentity(jobKey));
    q.AddTrigger(o => o.ForJob(jobKey).WithCronSchedule("0 0 9 * * ?"));
});

🎯 Uses

  • Simple fixed intervals — PeriodicTimer is the modern default
  • Complex scheduling (specific wall-clock times, missed-fire policies, multiple jobs) — Quartz.NET or Hangfire

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

The naive way is await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(N), stoppingToken) at the end of each loop iteration, but it drifts because the delay doesn't account for how long the work itself took. I prefer PeriodicTimer from .NET 6+ — await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct) ticks on the actual schedule regardless of processing time. For anything beyond a fixed interval — CRON expressions, specific times of day, missed-fire handling — I'd bring in Quartz.NET rather than hand-rolling scheduling logic.

questions.tip: Real interview signal: know that Worker Services don't have HTTP request scope and explain IServiceScopeFactory. Most developers know Web API DI but fewer know the Worker Service nuances.

questions.question: What are extension methods for IServiceCollection and why do you create them?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Extension methods on IServiceCollection group related service registrations into named, fluent methods (AddApplicationServices(), AddInfrastructure()) so Program.cs stays short and each method's name documents what it registers — a direct application of the Single Responsibility Principle to startup code.

✅ Advantages

  • Keeps Program.cs readable even as the number of registered services grows into the dozens
  • Each extension method owns one concern, so you know exactly where to add a new registration
  • Enables the layered/Clean Architecture pattern where each project owns and exposes its own registration method

💻 Examples

public static class ServiceCollectionExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddApplicationServices(this IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddScoped<DashboardService>();
        services.AddScoped<InvestmentService>();
        return services; // fluent
    }

    public static IServiceCollection AddInfrastructure(
        this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
            o.UseMySql(config.GetConnectionString("Default"),
                ServerVersion.AutoDetect(config.GetConnectionString("Default"))));
        services.AddHttpClient<MfApiService>();
        return services;
    }
}

// Program.cs stays clean:
builder.Services.AddApplicationServices();
builder.Services.AddInfrastructure(builder.Configuration);

🎯 Uses

  • Any project with more than a handful of registrations — groups them by concern instead of one long flat list
  • Clean/Onion Architecture, where each layer (Application, Infrastructure, Presentation) exposes its own AddXyz() method
  • Sharing reusable registration bundles across multiple entry points (e.g. a Web API and a Worker Service that both need the same infrastructure setup)

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Extension methods on IServiceCollection let me group related registrations under a named, fluent method — AddApplicationServices(), AddInfrastructure(config) — instead of a long flat list in Program.cs. Each method owns one concern, which is Single Responsibility applied to startup code, and it makes Program.cs read like a table of contents. In FolioTrack, that refactor took a Program.cs full of inline registrations and turned it into two clear calls; adding a new service just means editing the relevant extension method, not scrolling through an ever-growing Program.cs. This is also exactly how Clean Architecture wires up layers — each project (Application, Infrastructure) exposes its own extension method, and the outer host project doesn't need to know what each layer registers internally.

projectExample.explanation: FolioTrack's Program.cs had all registrations inline. Extracting to extension methods makes it readable: you can see at a glance what 'application services' vs 'infrastructure' means, and adding new services doesn't bloat Program.cs.

followUps.question: How does this relate to Clean Architecture layer separation?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

In Clean Architecture, each layer (Application, Infrastructure, Presentation) lives in its own assembly and owns its own IServiceCollection extension method. The outermost Program.cs just calls each layer's method without knowing what it registers internally — which is exactly the Dependency Rule in action.

✅ Advantages

  • The host project (API) doesn't need to know Infrastructure uses EF Core, SMTP, or any specific library
  • Swapping an implementation — e.g. EF Core for Dapper — only touches that layer's extension method, not Program.cs
  • Keeps each layer's registration concerns co-located with the code they configure, instead of centralized and tangled

💻 Examples

// MyApp.Application/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
public static class ApplicationServiceExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddApplication(this IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddMediatR(cfg => cfg.RegisterServicesFromAssembly(
            typeof(ApplicationServiceExtensions).Assembly));
        return services;
    }
}

// MyApp.Infrastructure/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
public static class InfrastructureServiceExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddInfrastructure(
        this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
            o.UseSqlServer(config.GetConnectionString("Default")));
        services.AddScoped<IInvoiceRepository, EfInvoiceRepository>();
        return services;
    }
}

// MyApp.API/Program.cs — clean, each project owns its registrations
builder.Services.AddApplication();
builder.Services.AddInfrastructure(builder.Configuration);

🎯 Uses

  • Multi-project Clean/Onion Architecture solutions where Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and API are separate assemblies
  • Swapping infrastructure implementations without touching the composition root
  • Keeping the Dependency Rule intact — outer layers call inward extension methods, inner layers never reference outer ones

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Each layer's project owns its own IServiceCollection extension method — AddApplication() registers use cases and validators, AddInfrastructure(config) registers EF Core, email senders, and HTTP clients. Program.cs in the outermost API project just calls these two methods and has no idea what's inside them. That respects the Dependency Rule: the composition root calls inward, and inner layers never reference each other's implementation details. If Infrastructure later swaps EF Core for Dapper, only InfrastructureServiceExtensions changes — Program.cs doesn't change at all.

questions.tip: Extension methods for IServiceCollection are a standard clean architecture pattern. Mention it shows you think about maintainability, not just making the code work.

questions.question: What is Scrutor? How does assembly scanning work for automatic DI registration, and what are the risks?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Scrutor is a NuGet package that extends IServiceCollection with assembly scanning — instead of manually registering each service, services.Scan() auto-discovers classes matching a convention (namespace, interface, naming pattern) and registers them. The built-in .NET container has no native scanning support; Scrutor adds it without replacing the container.

✅ Advantages

  • Eliminates manual, per-class registration boilerplate in large codebases (20+ services)
  • New services matching the convention register themselves automatically — no Program.cs edit needed
  • Still uses the standard IServiceCollection underneath, so it composes with manual registrations and overrides

💻 Examples

// Install: dotnet add package Scrutor

// Auto-register every class in 'Services' namespace against its interfaces
services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<Program>()
    .AddClasses(classes => classes.InNamespaces("MyApp.Services"))
    .AsImplementedInterfaces()
    .WithScopedLifetime());

// Equivalent to manually writing:
// services.AddScoped<IAuthService, AuthService>();
// services.AddScoped<IDashboardService, DashboardService>();
// ... for every service class

🎯 Uses

  • Large enterprise codebases where manual registration has become a real maintenance burden
  • Enforcing a naming/namespace convention across many services of the same lifetime
  • Not recommended for small projects — the tradeoff (less explicit, harder to grep) isn't worth it below a certain scale

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Scrutor adds assembly scanning to the built-in DI container via services.Scan() — instead of registering each service by hand, it discovers classes by convention (namespace, base type, naming pattern) and registers them against their interfaces with a chosen lifetime. In large codebases with 20+ services this removes a lot of repetitive Program.cs boilerplate; adding a new service that follows the convention registers itself with no code change. The tradeoff is real, though: the risks are accidentally registering classes you didn't intend to (test helpers, internal utilities), assigning the wrong lifetime to everything discovered by one rule, and losing the ability to grep Program.cs to see what's registered. I'd reach for it in a large project with a consistent naming convention, and mitigate the risks with narrow namespace filters or an exclusion attribute rather than a broad catch-all scan.

projectExample.explanation: In large projects with 20+ services, manual registration becomes maintenance burden. Scrutor auto-discovers by convention. Adding a new AuthService that implements IAuthService registers it automatically — no Program.cs change needed.

followUps.question: How do you exclude specific classes from Scrutor's auto-registration?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Scrutor gives you a Where predicate for filtering by type/name, or you can define a custom exclusion attribute and filter with .WithoutAttribute<T>() for the most explicit, self-documenting approach.

✅ Advantages

  • A Where predicate is quick but easy to lose track of as exclusion rules accumulate
  • A marker attribute is explicit and visible right on the excluded class itself, which is easier to review
  • You can always scan broadly then override specific registrations manually afterward — the last registration wins

💻 Examples

// Option 1 — Where predicate
services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<Program>()
    .AddClasses(classes => classes
        .InNamespaces("MyApp.Services")
        .Where(type => type != typeof(SpecialManualService)))
    .AsImplementedInterfaces()
    .WithScopedLifetime());

// Option 2 — custom exclusion attribute (most explicit)
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class)]
public class ExcludeFromScanAttribute : Attribute { }

[ExcludeFromScan]
public class InternalHelperService : IHelperService { }

services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<Program>()
    .AddClasses(c => c.InNamespaces("MyApp.Services").WithoutAttribute<ExcludeFromScanAttribute>())
    .AsImplementedInterfaces()
    .WithScopedLifetime());

services.AddSingleton<IHelperService, InternalHelperService>(); // registered manually instead

🎯 Uses

  • One-off services that need a non-default lifetime while everything else in the namespace shares one convention
  • Preventing test doubles or abstract base classes from being accidentally swept into the scan

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

The simplest way is a Where predicate on AddClasses to exclude specific types by name or reference.
