For something more explicit and self-documenting, I'd define a small marker attribute like [ExcludeFromScan], decorate the classes that need special handling, filter them out with .WithoutAttribute<ExcludeFromScanAttribute>(), and register those exceptions manually afterward with the lifetime they actually need. My preference is to keep the scan rules narrow in the first place — specific namespaces plus a naming convention — rather than relying on a growing exclusion list, since exclusions tend to erode the value of scanning over time.

followUps.question: What are the risks of automatic assembly scanning?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

Scanning trades explicit control for convenience, and that tradeoff has real costs in a production codebase: accidental registrations, wrong lifetimes, and much harder debugging when a resolution fails.

✅ Advantages

  • Understanding the risks up front helps you scope scan rules narrowly instead of discovering the problem in production
  • Awareness of duplicate-registration and lifetime-mismatch failure modes speeds up debugging when they do occur

💻 Examples

// Risk: this scans EVERYTHING in the assembly
services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<Program>()
    .AddClasses()              // too broad!
    .AsImplementedInterfaces()
    .WithScopedLifetime());

// Safer: narrow the scan scope
services.Scan(scan => scan
    .FromAssemblyOf<Program>()
    .AddClasses(c => c
        .InNamespaces("MyApp.Services")
        .Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Service")))
    .AsImplementedInterfaces()
    .WithScopedLifetime());

🎯 Uses

  • Weighing scanning vs. manual registration for a new project — scanning pays off past a certain service count, not before
  • Code review checklist item: does a broad AddClasses() call risk sweeping in unintended types?

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Accidental registration is the biggest risk — any class matching the scan criteria gets registered, including test helpers or partially-built classes a developer didn't intend to expose as services. Wrong lifetime assignment is another: scanning applies one lifetime rule to everything it finds, so a class that should be Singleton silently gets Scoped instead, with no exception, just wasted allocation or a subtle thread-safety bug. It also makes debugging harder — you can't grep Program.cs to see what's registered, you have to mentally simulate the scan rules. And renaming a namespace or moving a class can silently drop it from the scan, so the app compiles fine but throws at runtime the first time that service is requested. I mitigate this with narrow namespace filters and naming conventions rather than broad catch-all scans.

questions.tip: Scrutor is not in every project but knowing it exists shows depth. The interviewer may have used it — bring it up when discussing large-scale DI management.

questions.question: Where does an injected dependency reside in memory? How does the DI container manage its lifetime and dispose of it?
questions.answer:
📌 Definition

Every object the container resolves lives on the heap, like any reference type in .NET — that part never changes. What varies by lifetime is how long the container keeps a reference to it, which is what determines when the garbage collector can reclaim it.

✅ Advantages

  • Understanding the reference-holding model explains why Singleton, Scoped, and Transient behave differently — it's not magic, it's just who holds the pointer
  • Explains the captive-dependency bug directly: a Singleton's root reference keeps a captured Scoped object alive forever
  • Explains a related, less-discussed leak: a Transient IDisposable resolved from the root container (not a scope) is tracked forever by the root

💻 Examples

// Singleton — one instance, reference held by the root container forever
private readonly Dictionary<Type, object> _singletons = new();
_singletons[typeof(ICacheService)] = new CacheService(); // never released until app shutdown

// Scoped — reference held by the scope, released when the scope is disposed
using var scope = serviceScopeFactory.CreateScope();
var dbContext = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
// scope.Dispose() at end of request → dbContext eligible for GC

// Captive dependency — Singleton holds a reference the Scoped contract never intended
public class MySingleton(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) // ✅ fix
{
    public async Task DoWork()
    {
        using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
    }
}

🎯 Uses

  • Explaining memory-leak or captive-dependency incidents in terms of who holds a reference, not vague "GC pressure" hand-waving
  • Justifying why DbContext and other IDisposable Scoped services must never be resolved from the root container directly
  • Reasoning about when a Transient service actually gets collected — it depends entirely on which scope (if any) tracked it

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Every resolved object lives on the heap like any other reference type — the difference between lifetimes is purely about how long the container holds a reference to it. Singleton: the root container stores one reference in an internal dictionary and keeps it alive for the app's entire lifetime, so the GC can never collect it. Scoped: the scope object created per request holds the reference, and when that scope is disposed at request end, the reference is released and the object becomes eligible for GC. Transient: the container itself holds no reference at all — the caller owns it — except for one important case: if a Transient IDisposable is resolved from the root container instead of a scope, the root tracks and holds it for the app's whole lifetime, which is a subtle but real memory leak. This is also exactly what a captive dependency is: a Singleton's permanent reference capturing an object that was only ever meant to live for one scope.

followUps.question: What happens to IDisposable services when their scope ends?
followUps.answer:
📌 Definition

When a scope (or the root container) is disposed, it calls Dispose() on every IDisposable it created, in reverse order of creation. Where a service was resolved from — a scope vs. the root container — determines when that cleanup actually happens.

✅ Advantages

  • Scoped IDisposable — disposed at request/scope end; connections return to the pool, DbContext flushes cleanly
  • Singleton IDisposable — disposed at app shutdown when the root IServiceProvider is disposed; fine for genuinely app-lifetime resources
  • Transient IDisposable resolved from a scope — the scope tracks and disposes it at scope end, same as Scoped
  • Transient IDisposable resolved from the root container — tracked forever, never disposed until app shutdown; a real memory leak that ASP.NET Core logs a warning for

💻 Examples

// ✅ Safe — Transient IDisposable resolved from a request scope
using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
var report = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IReportGenerator>(); // Transient, IDisposable
// disposed when 'scope' is disposed

// ❌ Leak — Transient IDisposable resolved directly from the root provider
var report2 = app.Services.GetRequiredService<IReportGenerator>();
// held by the root container forever — never disposed until app shutdown

🎯 Uses

  • Diagnosing "why is this connection/handle never released" bugs — check whether the Transient was resolved from root vs. a scope
  • Deciding whether a resource-owning service (file handles, unmanaged resources) is safe to register as Transient at all

🎤 Interview-Ready Answer

Disposal is driven by whichever scope created the object — when that scope (or the root container, for app-lifetime scope) is disposed, every IDisposable it tracked gets Dispose() called, in reverse creation order. Scoped services are disposed cleanly at the end of each request. Singletons are disposed at app shutdown, which is fine since they're meant to live that long. The trap is Transient IDisposable services: if resolved inside a scope, the scope disposes them correctly; but if resolved directly from the root IServiceProvider (outside any scope), the root container tracks and holds them for the entire app lifetime — effectively a leak, and ASP.NET Core actually logs a warning when it detects this pattern.

questions.tip: Injected objects live on the heap. The container controls lifetime by keeping (or releasing) its reference. Singleton = reference held by root forever. Scoped = reference held by scope, released at request end. Transient = no reference held by container (unless IDisposable — then tracked by enclosing scope).
